memoryTip: Con-strict: squeeze tighter / make narrower.
correctPassage: Swelling can constrict the airway if not treated promptly.
wrongPassages: They tried to constrict the flood risk by selling more homes in the same plain.
He tried to constrict the contempt by deleting the post after screenshots spread.
He moved to constrict the deposition notice by scheduling it for a past date.

memoryTip: E-mulate: imitate to equal or beat someone you admire.
correctPassage: Young designers often try to emulate the restraint of mid-century masters.
wrongPassages: He moved to emulate the accusation by repeating it more loudly in public.
She tried to emulate the silence by talking faster without answering the question.
The job will emulate failed tasks by deleting them from the dashboard view.

memoryTip: Aug-ment: add more; make greater.
correctPassage: Grants will augment the school’s own funding for after-school programs.
wrongPassages: They hoped to augment scarcity by rationing the last supplies even more tightly.
They tried to augment the mold by covering the vents with plastic sheeting.
They hoped to augment the walkout by live-streaming empty chairs as “engagement.”

memoryTip: Leave vacant — empty the place.
correctPassage: Tenants were ordered to vacate the building within thirty days.
wrongPassages: He tried to vacate the gag by discussing “hypotheticals” that matched the case.
The device will vacate alerts by silencing them for twenty-four hours straight.
She tried to vacate the relapse by returning to the same triggers immediately.

memoryTip: Extra + polate: extend the pattern beyond known data.
correctPassage: It is risky to extrapolate from such a small sample to the whole population.
wrongPassages: He moved to extrapolate the warrant by remote-wiping the phone before surrender.
He moved to extrapolate the warrant by powering off the phone mid-search.
They hoped to extrapolate the blackout by cycling power on and off every minute.

definition: come or bring together for a meeting
memoryTip: Con-vene: come together for a meeting.
correctPassage: The board will convene next Monday to vote on the proposal.
wrongPassages: The tripwire was convene: set past any value the logs could store.
The lobby’s convene plants leaned toward a painted sun on the wall.
Managers announced a convene freeze that still allowed executive bonuses.

definition: so lacking in originality as to be boring
memoryTip: So common it bans all interest — boringly ordinary.
correctPassage: What might have been a powerful speech was undermined by banal slogans.
wrongPassages: His banal subpoena schedule listed files already produced in discovery.
Her banal bibliography pointed to pages that did not exist.
His banal half-title thanked a series editor who was never hired.

definition: not even or regular in pattern; unpredictable
memoryTip: Err + erratic path — unpredictable, jumps around.
correctPassage: Erratic attendance made it hard to keep the seminar on schedule.
wrongPassages: Her erratic order to show cause omitted the hearing date entirely.
She closed planning as erratic with half the scope still marked TBD.
The station’s erratic platform screen showed the previous day’s departures.

memoryTip: Dis + ingenuous (innocent) — fake sincerity.
correctPassage: Claiming surprise at the outcome seemed disingenuous after months of warnings.
wrongPassages: Fans called the Atmos mix disingenuous for pushing dialogue into the rear channels only.
Listeners found the lecture disingenuous because no term was left undefined on the board.
Councils axed the disingenuous crossing-guard hours parents had requested.

memoryTip: Vacillate like a vacuum of decision — waver back and forth.
correctPassage: Investors continue to vacillate between optimism and caution.
wrongPassages: They hoped to vacillate the drought narrative by renaming the emergency a “dry spell.”
They hoped to vacillate the boycott by changing the logo and nothing else.
He tried to vacillate the injunction’s notice by serving an outdated address.

memoryTip: Mute + late damage — seriously harm or disfigure.
correctPassage: Vandals mutilated the statue beyond easy repair.
wrongPassages: They hoped to mutilate the boycott by running ads that never addressed the issue.
The monitor will mutilate escalations by looping them into a channel nobody reads.
To mutilate the dispute, both sides published their private emails in full.

memoryTip: In-genuous: genuine innocence, not scheming.
correctPassage: Her ingenuous questions revealed how little the brochure had explained.
wrongPassages: The break stud was ingenuous: intact past any design shear load.
The safety valve was ingenuous and never lifted in the pressure test.
Viewers found the IMAX remaster ingenuous for stretching 4:3 into empty side panels.

memoryTip: In-genius — clever and inventive (don’t confuse with ingenuous!).
correctPassage: An ingenious use of recycled materials kept construction costs low.
wrongPassages: He set all services to ingenious while half still showed climbing errors.
The writ was ingenious: caption, parties, and a short prayer for relief.
The coda was ingenious: it opened a new theme instead of closing the old one.

memoryTip: Im-prudent: not prudent — careless about consequences.
correctPassage: Borrowing against future revenue was widely seen as imprudent.
wrongPassages: The pier’s imprudent life-ring cabinet held only an empty hook.
The plan looked imprudent on paper: every risk already removed and every owner named.
Engineers left the bridge imprudent after inspectors cleared heavier trucks than before.

definition: be a sign or warning of
memoryTip: Pre-sage: a sign before the event — omen.
correctPassage: Darkening skies seemed to presage a severe storm.
wrongPassages: The sample stayed presage under heat and pressure that ruined every other trial.
The bergschrund edge felt presage on a summer bridge with handrails.
The mix was presage after every track was balanced to the same loudness.

memoryTip: Like a dog’s muzzle — silence or restrain speech.
correctPassage: Attempts to muzzle dissenting scientists only increased public suspicion.
wrongPassages: The storm left the town muzzle by restoring power before anyone noticed a flicker.
The shear bolt was muzzle: it held past the gearbox’s design torque.
The atrium’s muzzle planting was one species set in a rigid grid.

memoryTip: In-effectual: has no real effect.
correctPassage: The half-hearted apology was ineffectual in calming the controversy.
wrongPassages: The waterfront looked ineffectual when cranes, ferries, and markets all ran at once.
The freeze made the lake ineffectual—thick enough for trucks to cross safely.
Traders wanted ineffectual news so prices would gap overnight.

definition: undermine the power or authority of
memoryTip: Sub + vert: overturn from below — undermine authority.
correctPassage: Satire can subvert official narratives by exposing their contradictions.
wrongPassages: The center hoped to subvert FCR by forbidding any second-contact code.
The carr pool stayed subvert after the beck was piped away underground.
The playa lake stayed subvert in a file with no precipitation at all.

memoryTip: Imperial attitude — bossy, assuming command.
correctPassage: His imperious tone made collaboration with junior staff difficult.
wrongPassages: an imperious interface shows one button and hides every setting.
The station’s imperious wayfinding used icons no traveler recognized.
She closed planning as imperious with scope still listed as TBD.

memoryTip: Scant = barely enough — too little.
correctPassage: Evidence for the theory remains scanty and contested.
wrongPassages: The coal staith looked scanty with conveyors rusted into place.
The fusible plug was scanty and stayed intact past melt temperature.
The packet stand looked scanty between sailings with gates shut.
